name: The medieval problem of universals (Roscelin, William of Champeaux, Abelard)
plain_explanation: When we call several different cats 'cats,' what, if anything, corresponds to the general word 'cat' itself? Roscelin said a universal like 'cat' is just a word, a puff of breath, with no reality beyond the individual cats. William of Champeaux, a realist, held universals have their own independent reality. Abelard, Roscelin's pupil, argued for a middle position: we do not predicate a bare physical word-sound of things, but a word as meaning; things genuinely resemble one another, and this resemblance gives rise to universals, but the resemblance itself is not a 'thing.' He also allowed that universals exist as patterns in God's mind prior to creation.
precise_definition: The scholastic debate over the ontological status of general terms (genera and species): whether they denote real, independently existing entities (realism), are mere names/vocal sounds with no corresponding reality (nominalism), or occupy some intermediate status as concepts grounded in real resemblances among particulars (Abelard's conceptualist-leaning position).
why_it_mattered: It is the central metaphysical/logical dispute of early scholasticism, made newly urgent by the twelfth-century discovery that Plato and Aristotle disagree about it, and it recurs, in more developed form, throughout the following two centuries of scholastic philosophy (Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Occam).
historical_origin: Sharpened in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries by Roscelin's controversial nominalism and Anselm's and Abelard's responses to it.
examples: Roscelin's charge that a universal is mere 'flatus vocis,' a physical event of speech
Abelard's reply that a 'flatus vocis' is itself a thing, so what is predicated must be the word as meaning, not the word as physical sound
Abelard's view that Platonic ideas exist as God's own concepts, patterns for creation, even though universals as such are not independently existing things
objections: Anselm's charge (against Roscelin) that if a universal is only a vocal event, then 'man' would not be a real unity but only a common name, an unacceptably extreme atomistic consequence
John of Salisbury 'laughed at' both Abelard's and Roscelin's theories of universals, suggesting contemporaries found neither fully satisfying
competing_positions: William of Champeaux's realism (universals have independent reality)
Roscelin's nominalism (universals are mere words/vocal sounds)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell judges Abelard's treatment 'certainly very able,' remarking that 'the most modern discussions of the problem of universals have not got much further'; the debate directly anticipates Aquinas's, Duns Scotus's, and Occam's later treatments.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Roscelin's nominalist leanings got him into theological trouble over the Trinity, since treating the Three Persons as three distinct substances risked tritheism.
